verdict:
Mostly sound, with a few reader-visible contradictions. I rebuilt the document with Python, and every {{placeholder}} matches graph-v4.json. I also recomputed analytics-v4.json from the graph and it matches exactly. No node is dated before a hard prerequisite. All 12 rows of the trunk table and every year and band in the 06 branch table match the graph. Almost every year, band and Plateau/Recursive contrast in the 12 branch narratives also matches. The 230-trial, 6 g helium-3, 1.1 kg/h, 2–9% and 2.6-year arithmetic checks out. Process counts match the work files: 722 changes accepted, 132 rejected, 173 facts flagged, 20 nodes added, 632 sources.

The problems are concentrated. (1) Program compression is given two ways. The hand-written text and the node title say "a quarter to a third" (25–33%), "at best". The node's own description, the scenario table, 04-two-clocks and the trunk narrative say 20–30% realized, with a 38% ceiling. (2) Qualification savings are given as "15–30%" for the base case. The node description and the physical-gate table put the base case at 10–20% (15% is the node's threshold, and 20–30% applies to Recursive). (3) The critical-path intro misstates what the table shows: only 13 of 39 paths run through public access, and none ends at a qualification gate. (4) Several "every scenario" and date claims contradict the graph: low-orbit safety at 100,000 satellites is 2031 in Recursive, the graph lists three Mars windows, the qualified-checker date in the open questions is wrong, the Plateau definition is wrong, and on-demand math is dated 2027 instead of 2028. (5) The rendered reviewer-dispute text is stale for four nodes. The other findings are low-severity wording and title-matching fixes.

lens: Analyst grounding and facts (ai-math-frontier-analyst rules: pathway and band on implications, conditional wording for T1/T2, no practical galactic speedups, written chains for hardware outcomes, bands as judgments, catalog families only, trust tiers capped at T3 as of 2026-10-07, correct release statistics) plus a fact-check of load-bearing empirical claims.
verdict: The grounding is mostly sound. All 42 families cited in the graph and every family number in the narratives appear in ref-family-catalog. Most narrative tier labels match the Lean flags and the graph's statement-gap notes. Galactic speedups (107, 130, 109) are never treated as practical. The release statistics are right (722 manuscripts, 372 families, 127 with Lean, about 4,000 problems, unreleased model, 3 of 16 PDE and 5 of 6 logic families formalized). Bands are called judgments throughout. The regulator cap is respected, with one exception that the graph explains (cap-research-math-public). The hand-written tables match the graph: I checked all 12 rows of the trunk table and every node in the 06 summary table that matched a graph title exactly, and found no mismatch. The Amdahl figures (18/38/51%) reproduce. Three problems need fixing before handoff. (1) The builder labels node tiers "T0" to "T7". About 500 labels such as "(T5 · 2029 · Medium)" read as trust tiers T4/T5 and contradict "nothing above T3". (2) 02-method says the model uses the framework's bands but does not disclose two departures. Most nodes sit above their pathway default: by my count 206 of 350 non-exogenous nodes in Exponential, and 88 even in Plateau. The trunk node "Research-grade math for outside teams" is High in every scenario despite the framework's public-model cap and its regulatory gate, and 256 nodes sit downstream of it. (3) The written-chain rule is met only for tiers 6–7. Ten tier-5 flight demonstrations rated Medium have no written chain. I fact-checked 20 empirical claims against primary sources, 33FG/Mach33 and the research files. Fourteen held up: Mach33's $4,915/$656/~$300 per kg path, AI1 solar at 56% and 71 kW/t, the V3 10x capacity step, Vero 27/43, Ilin's 10 days, $200 and 229 prompts, the Perseverance AI-planned drives of Dec 8 and 10 2025, the Peregrine valve, three failed relights on Flight 13, the NASA UQ paper's 2040–2050, second-order self-force existing only for circular Schwarzschild orbits, the NP-hardness in arXiv 2601.21914, the AEPS paper's "100% test with 50% margin by analysis", the FY2026 $24.4B against the FY2027 request of $18.8B, and Astra's ~$2,000 for ten results. Two were contradicted. 09-nil says two Mars windows remain before end-2031 when there are three, and it calls 460 s the hydrogen-oxygen Isp limit when RL10B-2 flies at 465.5 s. Four were overstated or unqualified: HELIOS "11 of 11" counts compilation success only; seL4's 25 person-years covered design and implementation as well as proof; the Kingy Comparator run was a tech blog's run with no statement audit; and the Mach33 SpaceX-equity disclosure is missing.

lens: Editor for the paper writer and readers: clarity, jargon, redundancy, structure, signposting, consistent terminology, house style. Numbers were cross-checked with Python against graph-v4.json and work/analytics-v4.json.
verdict:
Partly. The substance a writer needs is there. It has a clear thesis (two clocks), three explicit scenarios, dated and banded nodes, the strongest counter-case for every branch, a nil-effects section, signposts, assumptions and recorded disputes. The section most worth lifting is the Bottom line plus sections 3, 8 and 9.

The document still needs work before a writer can use it safely.

1. Some headline sentences contradict their own data.
   - Section 3 says the provable-to-flyable gap "widens", but its own counts narrow it from 77 to 49 nodes.
   - Section 7 says most critical paths run through public access. Only 13 of 39 do, and 14 have no AI-math step at all. That is itself a strong, buried finding.
   - Program compression appears as "a quarter to a third at best", as "20–30%" and as a "38%" ceiling.
   - "The physical half barely moves" overstates a shift of 0.8–1.0 years against 1.1–1.7.
2. The notation and wording invite misreading.
   - Node tiers and trust tiers share the "T" prefix.
   - "Likely" is used for Medium (30–70%).
   - Earliest credible years read as forecasts, and the warning comes about 1,900 lines later.
   - Scenario names alternate with S1/S2/S3, and "certified", "guaranteed" and "honest" error bars are never distinguished.
3. Jargon is unglossed. Lean, Comparator, Hexagon, galactic, unforced Navier–Stokes and the gate names are all used without definitions. About 150 internal node IDs, tl-position tags and process notes ("the client", "A1 merged…", "the paper should say so in advance") leak into generated text.
4. The 2,900-line structure buries the argument. The cross-cutting findings come after about 1,550 lines of branch detail, and every branch states its hook facts two or three times.
5. There is a lot of repetition across sections:
   - "Space's own exponential is physical" appears in four places.
   - The catalog-family sentence appears verbatim in both the Bottom line and Finding 1.
   - The audit counts (173 flagged, about 40 corrected) appear in both sections 1 and 11.

What the writer still lacks:

1. **A glossary** (finding 9 drafts one).
2. **A claim-to-source map** for the 25–30 numbers the paper will quote. Sources are listed only by domain, and two rows in the capability-ladder table cite only "Analyst timeline".
3. **A quotable-numbers list** that shows each figure's audit status from work/facts-flagged.txt.
4. **A chart-ready table of the two-clocks curve.** The cumulative share by year, tier group and scenario is computed in analytics but never rendered, and it is the natural lead figure.
5. **A decision on disclosure.** This covers the commissioning premise ("client") and the heavy reliance on Mach33/33FG launch-cost sources; the claim that those pages disclose SpaceX holdings is itself marked unverified.
6. **A short "what this means for whom" section.** It should cover operators, agencies, insurers and investors, beyond the adoption order in Finding 5.

Moving section 8 to follow section 3 (in doc/_skeleton.md), or at least adding the reading path in finding 8, would let the writer find the argument quickly.

**Terms used throughout.**

- *Lean* is a proof language in which a computer checks every step. *Mathlib* is its shared library.
